'''''Eclipta prostrata''''', the '''false daisy''' or '''tattoo plant''', is a species of plant in the family [[Asteraceae]].<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN |access-date=5 August 2024}}</ref><ref name="usda">{{cite web |title=''Eclipta prostrata'' L. |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/plant-profile/ECPR |publisher=Plants Database, Natural Resources Conservation Service, US Department of Agriculture |access-date=25 August 2026 |date=2026}}</ref> It is widespread across much of the world.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=111273|publisher=eFlora, Flora of North America|title=''Eclipta'' Linnaeus, Mant. Pl. 157, 286. 1771|date=2026|access-date=24 August 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200023875|publisher=eFlora, Flora of China|title=''Eclipta prostrata'' L., Mant. Pl. 2: 286. 1771|date=2026|access-date=24 August 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=eclipta+prostrata|publisher=Altervista Flora Italiana|title=''Eclipta prostrata'' L.|date=2026|access-date=24 August 2026 }}</ref>

This species is native to North and South America. It also grows commonly in moist places in warm temperate to tropical areas worldwide. It can be found in habitats such as on marsh edges, along lake shores and river banks, and in brackish marshes and cypress depression swamps. It is considered to be a weed.<ref name="Weeds of the South" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Everitt |first1=J.H. |last2=Lonard |first2=R.L. |last3=Little |first3=C.R. |title=Weeds in South Texas and Northern Mexico |publisher=Texas Tech University Press |location=Lubbock |year=2007}} {{ISBN|0-89672-614-2}}</ref>
[[File:Eclipta prostrata at Kadavoor.jpg|thumb|180px|''E. prostrata'', India]]

==Description==
This plant has fibrous cylindrical, grayish roots from a shallow taproot. Solid, circular, purplish stems with white fine hairs, and grows between 0.3 and 1.5 m in height. [[Leaf|Leaves]] arranged in opposite pairs, hairy in two-sided, lanceolate, serrated 2–12.5 cm long, 5–35 mm wide.
The solitary perfect [[flower heads]] are {{convert|6–8|mm|abbr=on}} in diameter, with white florets. The bumpy achenes are compressed and narrowly winged with the papus attached at the apex, as well as an inconspicuous tuft of small trichomes.<ref name="Weeds of the South">{{cite book |last1=Bryson |first1=Charles T. |title=Weeds of the South |date=2009 |publisher=University of Georgia Press |location=Athens, Geogia |isbn=0-8203-3046-9 }}</ref><ref name="steenis1981">[[Cornelis Gijsbert Gerrit Jan van Steenis|Steenis, CGGJ van]] (1981). ''Flora, untuk sekolah di Indonesia''. PT Pradnya Paramita, Jakarta. pp. 423-424</ref>

== Traditional uses ==

The plant has [[traditional medicine|traditional uses]] in [[Ayurveda]]. In Hindi speaking regions of India, it is known as ''bhangra'' or ''bhringaraj''. ''[[Wedelia calendulacea]]'' is known by the same names, so the white-flowered ''E. alba'' is called white ''bhangra'' and the yellow-flowered ''W. calendulacea'' is called yellow ''bhangra''.<ref>Puri, H. S. 2003. ''Rasayana: Ayurvedic Herbs for Longevity and Rejuvenation''. Taylor & Francis, London. pages 80–85.</ref>

In [[Southeast Asia]], the dried whole plant is used in traditional medicine,<ref>{{cite book | editor1=Nantana Sittichai | editor2=Chayan Picheansoothon | date=2014 | title=Herbal Medicines Used in Primary Health Care in ASEAN | publisher=Department for Development of Thai Traditional and Alternative Medicine | isbn=978-616-11-2211-9 | pages=148–149 }}</ref> although there is no high-quality [[clinical research]] to indicate such uses are effective. The [[Balinese people|Balinese]] cook it as a vegetable, the [[Javanese people|Javanese]] consume this herb (''[[:ms:Urang-aring|orang-aring]]'' or ''urang-aring'') as part of their ''[[lalap]]'', they also infuse it with coconut oil as a kind of hair oil popular until the 1970s<ref name="heyne">[[Karel Heyne|Heyne, Karel]] (1987). ''Tumbuhan Berguna Indonesia'', vol. '''3''': p. 1833. Yayasan Sarana Wana Jaya, Jakarta</ref> Its leaves are extracted as a black hair dye, and in tattooing.<ref>Jukema, J., N.Wulijarni-Soetjipto, R.H.M.J. Lemmens & J.W.Hildebrand (1991). {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20160304193205/http://www.proseanet.org/prosea/e-prosea_detail.php?frt=&id=14 ''Eclipta alba'' (L.) Hassk.]}} Internet Record from Proseabase. Lemmens, R.H.M.J. and Wulijarni-Soetjipto, N. (Editors). PROSEA (Plant Resources of South-East Asia) Foundation, Bogor, Indonesia</ref>
